resources.string: all praise (al-ḥamdu)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_ism_spot
string-array.item: It can take ال: ٱلۡحَمۡدُ, ٱلۡقَدۡرِ.
It can take tanwīn: كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ.
It can follow a preposition, and then ends in jarr: لِلَّهِ, فِي لَيۡلَةِ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_ism_how
string-array.item: A noun names something without tying it to a time: رَبّ “Lord”, رَحۡمَة “mercy”, يَوۡم “day”.
It covers more than an English noun: pronouns (هُوَ), pointing words (هَٰذَا), adjectives (كَبِير) and words like فَوۡقَ “above” are all nouns.
Every noun has a gender and a number, is definite or not, and has a case ending. These are the next units.

resources.string: A verb is tied to a time: قَالَ “he said” is past. قَوۡل “a saying” names the same idea as a noun, with no time.
He did not beget (lam yalid)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_fil_spot
string-array.item: قَدۡ, سَـ, سَوۡفَ or لَمۡ can come before it: سَوۡفَ تَعۡلَمُونَ, لَمۡ يَلِدۡ.
Endings that say who did it: ـتُ “I”, ـتَ “you”, ـُوا “they”.
The silent تۡ of “she”: تَبَّتۡ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_fil_how
string-array.item: A verb is an action or a happening tied to a time.
There are three kinds: past (قَالَ “he said”), present and future (يَقُولُ “he says”), and command (قُلۡ “say”).
A verb has its doer built in: يَلِدۡ is “he begets”, with “he” in the يَـ.

resources.string: مُؤۡمِن “believer” comes from the verb ءَامَنَ “he believed”, but it takes ال and tanwīn and has no time, so it is a noun.
in the Night of Decree (fī laylati l-qadr)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_harf_spot
string-array.item: It takes neither ال nor tanwīn, and none of a verb’s endings.
Its ending never changes: فِي is always فِي.
Some are one letter joined to the next word: the بِ of بِسۡمِ, the وَ of وَٱلۡعَصۡرِ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_harf_how
string-array.item: A particle means something only with the words around it: فِي “in” needs something after it.
Some change the next word’s ending: فِي puts لَيۡلَةِ in jarr, and لَمۡ puts يَلِدۡ in jazm.
Others only join or add meaning: وَ “and”, ثُمَّ “then”, and هَلۡ, which asks a question.

resources.string: مَنۡ “who” is short too, but it stands for a person, so it is a noun. A particle never stands for a person or a thing.
O soul at peace (yā ayyatuha n-nafsu l-muṭmaʾinnah)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_gender_spot
string-array.item: Most feminine nouns end in ة: رَحۡمَة, جَنَّة.
Some end in ـَىٰ: ٱلۡحُسۡنَىٰ “the best”, ٱلۡأُخۡرَىٰ “the other”.
Some have no sign and are learned one by one: نَفۡس “soul”, شَمۡس “sun”, نَار “fire”, أَرۡض “earth”. They take هَٰذِهِ, the feminine “this”.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_gender_how
string-array.item: Every noun is masculine or feminine, things included.
Words that describe it or point to it match it: ٱلنَّفۡسُ ٱلۡمُطۡمَئِنَّةُ, and even يَٰٓأَيَّتُهَا takes a feminine ة.
Pronouns match too: وَٱلشَّمۡسِ وَضُحَىٰهَا “by the sun and its morning brightness”, where ـهَا is “her”.

resources.string: As a reading point, ة is said as t when you carry on and h when you stop. Here it matters as the usual sign of a feminine noun.
the two hands of Abū Lahab (yadā abī lahab)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_dual_spot
string-array.item: ـَانِ at the end in rafʿ: جَنَّتَانِ “two gardens”.
ـَيۡنِ in naṣb and jarr: ٱلنَّجۡدَيۡنِ “the two ways”.
Before another noun the ن drops: يَدَا أَبِي, not يَدَانِ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_dual_how
string-array.item: The dual means exactly two. Add ـَانِ or ـَيۡنِ to the singular; a ة becomes ت: جَنَّة, جَنَّتَانِ.
Its ending shows the case with a letter instead of a vowel (unit 3).
Pronouns and verbs have duals too: هُمَا “they both”.

resources.string: ـَيۡنِ has a fatḥa before the yāʾ and means two: ٱلنَّجۡدَيۡنِ. ـِينَ has a kasra before it and means many: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ.
the disbelievers (al-kāfirūn)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_sound_masc_plural_spot
string-array.item: ـُونَ at the end in rafʿ: ٱلۡكَٰفِرُونَ.
ـِينَ in naṣb and jarr: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ.
Before another noun the ن drops.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_sound_masc_plural_how
string-array.item: It is the plural of men, and of words describing them, with the singular kept whole: كَافِر, كَافِرُونَ.
Many are doer nouns: مُؤۡمِن “believer”, مُؤۡمِنُونَ.
A few words are treated like it without being one, such as ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ “the worlds”.

resources.string: ـِينَ has a kasra before the yāʾ and means many: ٱلضَّآلِّينَ. ـَيۡنِ has a fatḥa before it and means two: ٱلنَّجۡدَيۡنِ.
and did righteous deeds (wa ʿamilu ṣ-ṣāliḥāt)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_sound_fem_plural_spot
string-array.item: ـَات at the end: ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتِ, ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ.
In the Quran’s spelling the ā is often a small alif: ـَٰت.
A ة in the singular drops: صَالِحَة, صَالِحَات.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_sound_fem_plural_how
string-array.item: It is the usual plural of nouns ending in ة, and of some others: سَمَآء, سَمَٰوَٰت.
In rafʿ it ends in a ḍamma, and in both naṣb and jarr in a kasra: ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ is in naṣb here, as what they did.
It isn’t only about women: here ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ are good deeds.

resources.string: Not every ات is this ending. In ٱلۡأَصۡوَٰتِ “the voices” the ت is part of the root ص و ت, so it is a broken plural of صَوۡت.
in crowds (afwājā)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_broken_plural_spot
string-array.item: The word itself is reshaped, with no ending added: فَوۡج, أَفۡوَاج; رَجُل, رِجَال; كِتَاب, كُتُب.
Common shapes: أَفۡعَال (أَفۡوَاج), فِعَال (رِجَال), فُعُل (كُتُب), فُعَلَاء (عُلَمَاء).

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_broken_plural_how
string-array.item: The plural can’t be worked out for sure from the singular, so learn each noun with its plural.
It takes the ordinary vowel endings of a singular: أَفۡوَاجًا is in naṣb, with tanwīn.
A plural of things is treated as one feminine thing: تِلۡكَ ٱلۡأَيَّامُ “those days”, with تِلۡكَ, the feminine singular “that”.

resources.string: A sound plural keeps the singular whole and adds an ending: مُؤۡمِن, مُؤۡمِنُونَ. A broken plural changes the inside of the word.
with the hardship is ease (maʿa l-ʿusri yusrā)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_definiteness_spot
string-array.item: ال makes a noun definite: ٱلۡعُسۡرِ “the hardship”.
Tanwīn usually shows an indefinite noun: يُسۡرًا “ease”. But a name can have tanwīn and still be definite: مُحَمَّدٞ.
A noun joined to a definite noun after it (iḍāfa) is definite without ال: رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_definiteness_how
string-array.item: Definite (maʿrifa) means a particular one. Indefinite (nakira) means any one of its kind.
Always definite: names (ٱللَّهُ), pronouns (هُوَ), pointing words (هَٰذَا), “the one who” words (ٱلَّذِي), and nouns with ال.
It carries meaning: many scholars noted that ٱلۡعُسۡرِ in 94:5–6 is the same hardship both times, while يُسۡرًا, without ال, is a new ease each time.

resources.string: As a reading point, tanwīn is the n sound at the end of a word. Here it matters as the usual sign of an indefinite noun.
and the earth brings out its burdens (wa akhrajati l-arḍu athqālahā)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_cases_spot
string-array.item: Rafʿ usually ends in a ḍamma: ٱلۡأَرۡضُ.
Naṣb usually ends in a fatḥa: أَثۡقَالَهَا.
Jarr usually ends in a kasra: فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ.
With tanwīn the mark is doubled: أَحَدٌ, كُفُوًا, لَهَبٍ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_cases_how
string-array.item: A noun’s ending shows its job in the sentence, not its meaning: here ٱلۡأَرۡضُ is the one bringing out, so it is in rafʿ.
Rafʿ is for the doer, the subject and what is said about it; naṣb for the object and many others; jarr after a preposition, or as the second noun of an iḍāfa.
So words can change places and you still know who did what: the endings tell you.

resources.string: These are the same three marks as the short vowels. On the last letter of a noun they also show its case; inside a word they are only its sounds.
and We showed him the two ways (wa hadaynāhu n-najdayn)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_dual_plural_endings_spot
string-array.item: The dual: ـَانِ in rafʿ, ـَيۡنِ in naṣb and jarr. Here ٱلنَّجۡدَيۡنِ is in naṣb.
The sound masculine plural: ـُونَ in rafʿ, ـِينَ in naṣb and jarr.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_dual_plural_endings_how
string-array.item: These nouns show their case with a letter: ا or و for rafʿ, ي for naṣb and jarr.
Naṣb and jarr look the same, so the word’s job tells you which one it is.
The ن at the end doesn’t change with the case, and it drops before another noun.

resources.string: The sound feminine plural keeps vowel endings: a ḍamma in rafʿ, and a kasra in both naṣb and jarr.
Abū Lahab (abī lahab)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_five_nouns_spot
string-array.item: أَب “father”, أَخ “brother” and ذُو “owner of” (and the rare حَم and فُو), followed by another word.
Their case is a long vowel: و in rafʿ (أَبُو), ا in naṣb (أَبَا), ي in jarr (أَبِي).

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_five_nouns_how
string-array.item: The name Abū Lahab is written أَبِي لَهَبٖ in 111:1, because it is in jarr: “the hands of Abū Lahab”.
This happens only when another word follows. On its own, أَب takes ordinary vowels.
ذُو shows it often: ذُو ٱلۡعَرۡشِ “Owner of the Throne” (85:15) is in rafʿ.

resources.string: Duals and sound plurals also show their case with a letter, but they add an ending. The five nouns only lengthen their last vowel.
He is Allah (huwa llāh)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_detached_pronoun_spot
string-array.item: A pronoun written as a word of its own: هُوَ “he”, هِيَ “she”, هُمۡ “they”, أَنتَ “you”, نَحۡنُ “we”, أَنَا “I”.
It is often the subject at the start of a sentence: هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_detached_pronoun_how
string-array.item: It stands for someone already known: the speaker, the one spoken to, or someone absent.
It changes with person, gender and number: أَنتَ “you (a man)”, أَنتِ “you (a woman)”, أَنتُمۡ “you all”.
Every pronoun is definite, and its ending never changes.

resources.string: An attached pronoun is joined to the end of another word: رَبُّهُۥ “his Lord”. A detached one stands alone: هُوَ.
We have given you (aʿṭaynāka)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_attached_pronoun_spot
string-array.item: A short ending joined to a word: ـهُ “him, his”, ـهَا “her”, ـكَ “you, your”, ـنَا “us, our”, ـهُمۡ “them, their”, ـي “me, my”.
It can join a noun (رَبُّكَ), a verb (أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ) or a particle (عَلَيۡهِمۡ).

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_attached_pronoun_how
string-array.item: On a noun it is the owner: لِرَبِّكَ “to your Lord”.
On a verb it can be the doer or the object: in أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ, نَا is “We” who gave, and كَ is “you”, the one given to.
On a preposition it is what the preposition is about: عَلَيۡهِمۡ “upon them”.

resources.string: A detached pronoun stands alone as its own word: هُوَ “he”. An attached one can’t: ـهُ always joins another word.
You alone we worship (iyyāka naʿbudu)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_iyya_spot
string-array.item: إِيَّا with an attached pronoun: إِيَّاكَ, إِيَّاهُ, إِيَّانَا.
It comes before its verb, as the verb’s object.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_iyya_how
string-array.item: An object pronoun is usually joined to its verb: نَعۡبُدُكَ “we worship You”.
To put the object first, the pronoun needs a word to carry it: that is إِيَّا.
Putting it first adds “alone”: we worship You and no one else.

resources.string: هُوَ and أَنتَ stand alone as the subject. إِيَّاكَ stands alone too, but as the object.
and this city (wa hādhā l-balad)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_demonstrative_spot
string-array.item: Near: هَٰذَا “this” (masculine), هَٰذِهِۦ (feminine), هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ “these”.
Far: ذَٰلِكَ “that” (masculine), تِلۡكَ (feminine), أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ “those”.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_demonstrative_how
string-array.item: Before a noun with ال it means “this …”: هَٰذَا ٱلۡبَلَدِ “this city”.
Before a noun without ال it makes a sentence: هَٰذَا بَلَدٌ “this is a city”.
ذَٰلِكَ “that” can point to something near to show its greatness: ذَٰلِكَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبُ (2:2).

resources.string: هَٰذَا points by itself. ٱلَّذِي “the one who” also points to someone, but needs a sentence after it to complete it.
those whom You have blessed (alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_relative_spot
string-array.item: ٱلَّذِي (masculine), ٱلَّتِي (feminine), ٱلَّذِينَ (masculine plural); مَنۡ for people and مَا for things.
A sentence follows it and completes it: ٱلَّذِينَ أَنۡعَمۡتَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_relative_how
string-array.item: On its own it isn’t complete: “those who …” needs the sentence after it (the ṣila).
That sentence often has a pronoun pointing back to it: the ـهِمۡ of عَلَيۡهِمۡ is “those”.
Together they work as one noun: “the ones You have blessed”.

resources.string: هَٰذَا “this” points by itself. ٱلَّذِي “the one who” needs the sentence after it.
I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind (aʿūdhu bi-rabbi n-nās)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_preposition_spot
string-array.item: Words of their own: فِي “in”, مِنۡ “from”, إِلَىٰ “to”, عَلَىٰ “on”, عَنۡ “about, away from”.
One letter joined to the next word: بِـ “with, by, in”, لِـ “for, to”, كَـ “like”.
The noun after it ends in jarr: بِرَبِّ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_preposition_how
string-array.item: A preposition and its noun make a phrase that adds where, when, how or to whom: بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ “in the Lord of mankind”.
It can take an attached pronoun instead of a noun: بِهِۦ “with it”, عَلَيۡهِمۡ “upon them”.
A phrase like this can say something about a subject: ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ “praise is for Allah”.

resources.string: مِنۡ with a kasra is “from”, a preposition. مَنۡ with a fatḥa is “who”, a noun.
to your Lord (li-rabbika)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_pronoun_possessor_spot
string-array.item: A noun with an attached pronoun at its end: رَبِّكَ, دِينِكُمۡ.
The noun has no ال and no tanwīn.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_pronoun_possessor_how
string-array.item: The pronoun is the owner, like the second noun of an iḍāfa: رَبِّكَ is “the Lord of you”.
The pronoun makes the noun definite: “your Lord”, not “a lord”.
The noun keeps its own case: in لِرَبِّكَ it is in jarr after لِـ.

resources.string: In an iḍāfa the owner is a noun: رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ. Here it is a pronoun: رَبِّكَ.
the straight path (aṣ-ṣirāṭa l-mustaqīm)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_adjective_spot
string-array.item: It comes after the noun it describes: ٱلصِّرَٰطَ ٱلۡمُسۡتَقِيمَ.
It has the same ending as its noun: both end in a fatḥa here.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_adjective_how
string-array.item: It matches its noun in four things: case, definite or not, number and gender.
A plural of things takes a feminine singular adjective: وَفُرُشٖ مَّرۡفُوعَةٍ “and raised couches” (56:34).
An adjective is itself a noun, so it takes ال and tanwīn like one.

resources.string: Two nouns side by side can also be an iḍāfa: رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ. There the first has no ال and the second is in jarr; an adjective copies its noun instead.
He taught man what he did not know (ʿallama l-insāna mā lam yaʿlam)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_root_spot
string-array.item: Take away the extra letters and the vowels, and three letters are left: عَلَّمَ and يَعۡلَمۡ both come from ع ل م.
The same three letters, in the same order, come back in related words: عِلۡم “knowledge”, عَلِيم “all-knowing”.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_root_how
string-array.item: Most Arabic words are built on a root of three letters that carries a core meaning: ع ل م is about knowing.
Patterns build words around it: عَلِمَ “he knew”, عَلَّمَ “he taught”, عِلۡم “knowledge”.
Learn a root once and you know part of every word built on it. The Words tab shows each word’s root.

resources.string: The root is the three letters that carry the meaning. The pattern is the shape around them, measured with ف ع ل.
Master (māliki)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_pattern_spot
string-array.item: Words are measured with the letters ف ع ل: مَٰلِك is on فَاعِل, like كَافِر and عَالِم.
The extra letters and vowels of a word show in its pattern: مَغۡضُوب is on مَفۡعُول, رَحِيم on فَعِيل.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_pattern_how
string-array.item: A pattern carries a meaning of its own: فَاعِل is the one who does, مَفۡعُول the one it is done to, فَعِيل often a lasting quality.
Put a root into a pattern to make a word: م ل ك on فَاعِل gives مَالِك “owner, master”.
Knowing the pattern tells you what kind of word it is, even before you know its meaning.

resources.string: The pattern is the shape; the root is the three letters inside it that carry the meaning.
how your Lord dealt (kayfa faʿala rabbuka)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_past_spot
string-array.item: The basic form of a verb, with no prefix: فَعَلَ, خَلَقَ, قَالَ.
Endings that say who did it: فَعَلۡتُ “I did”, فَعَلۡنَا “we did”, فَعَلُوا “they did”, فَعَلَتۡ “she did”.
قَدۡ often comes before it: قَدۡ أَفۡلَحَ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_past_how
string-array.item: It tells of something that has happened: فَعَلَ “he did”.
With no ending it means “he”, and a noun doer comes after it: فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ “your Lord did”.
In the Quran it can also tell of something to come, to show it is certain: أَتَىٰٓ أَمۡرُ ٱللَّهِ “the command of Allah has come” (16:1).

resources.string: The present has a prefix for who does it: يَفۡعَلُ “he does”. The past has none, only endings: فَعَلَ.
You have blessed (anʿamta)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_doer_in_verb_spot
string-array.item: A past verb’s ending can be its doer: the ـتَ of أَنۡعَمۡتَ is “you”.
Others: ـتُ “I”, ـنَا “we”, ـُوا “they”, ـتُمۡ “you all”.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_doer_in_verb_how
string-array.item: When the doer is a pronoun, it is joined to the verb: أَنۡعَمۡتَ alone is a whole sentence, “you blessed”.
A noun doer comes after the verb instead: فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ.
An ending that isn’t the verb’s own person is its object: in ٱهۡدِنَا, نَا is “us”, the ones guided.

resources.string: Not every pronoun on a verb is its doer: in أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ, نَا is the doer and كَ is the object.
I do not worship what you worship (lā aʿbudu mā taʿbudūn)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_present_spot
string-array.item: A prefix at the start: أَ “I”, نَ “we”, يَ “he”, تَ “you” or “she”: أَعۡبُدُ, تَعۡبُدُونَ.
The four prefix letters spell أَنَيۡتُ, an easy way to remember them.
Some add an ending too: ـُونَ for “they” or “you all”.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_present_how
string-array.item: It is an action now or to come: أَعۡبُدُ “I worship, I will worship”.
Its usual ending is a ḍamma: أَعۡبُدُ. Some words before it change that ending (the next two concepts).
سَـ or سَوۡفَ make it clearly future: سَوۡفَ تَعۡلَمُونَ “you will come to know”.

resources.string: The past has no prefix, only endings: عَبَدۡتُمۡ “you worshipped”. The present starts with one: تَعۡبُدُونَ.
no one will ever have power over him (lan yaqdira ʿalayhi aḥad)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_subjunctive_spot
string-array.item: أَنۡ “to, that”, لَنۡ “will never”, كَيۡ or لِـ “so that”, or حَتَّىٰ “until” comes before a present verb.
The verb ends in a fatḥa: يَقۡدِرَ.
An ending ـُونَ loses its ن: لَن تَنَالُواْ ٱلۡبِرَّ “you will never attain righteousness” (3:92).

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_subjunctive_how
string-array.item: These words put the present verb in naṣb.
لَنۡ denies the future strongly: “will never”.
أَنۡ and its verb work together like one noun: أَن يُخَفِّفَ “to lighten” (4:28).

resources.string: أَنۡ with a sukūn comes before a verb and puts it in naṣb. أَنَّ with a shadda comes before a noun.
Did We not expand (a-lam nashraḥ)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_jussive_spot
string-array.item: لَمۡ “did not”, لَا “do not”, the لِـ of command, or a condition like إِن “if” comes before a present verb.
The verb ends in a sukūn: نَشۡرَحۡ, يَلِدۡ.
Or it loses a letter: ـُونَ loses its ن, and a long vowel can drop: لَمۡ يَكُن, from يَكُونُ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_jussive_how
string-array.item: لَمۡ turns a present verb into a denied past: لَمۡ يَلِدۡ “He did not beget”.
أَلَمۡ asks “did … not?” and expects a yes: أَلَمۡ نَشۡرَحۡ “did We not expand?”.
This sukūn is written, so it is read even when you don’t stop.

resources.string: The sukūn is a reading mark. At the end of a present verb it is also a sign of jazm.
He has succeeded (qad aflaḥa)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_qad_sa_spot
string-array.item: قَدۡ before a past verb: قَدۡ أَفۡلَحَ.
سَـ joined to a present verb, or سَوۡفَ before it: سَوۡفَ تَعۡلَمُونَ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_qad_sa_how
string-array.item: قَدۡ with a past verb stresses that it really happened: “has indeed”.
سَـ and سَوۡفَ make a present verb future: “will”.
Before a present verb, قَدۡ can mean “sometimes”, or stress that it is sure: قَدۡ يَعۡلَمُ ٱللَّهُ “Allah surely knows” (24:63).

resources.string: سَـ is joined to its verb, so don’t take it for a root letter: in سَيَصۡلَىٰ (111:3) it is “will”, and the verb is يَصۡلَىٰ.
Read! (iqraʾ)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_command_spot
string-array.item: It has no present prefix: from تَقۡرَأُ “you read” comes ٱقۡرَأۡ “read!”.
It ends in a sukūn, or loses a letter: ٱقۡرَأۡ, قُلۡ (from تَقُولُ).
To a group it ends in ـُوا: ٱعۡبُدُوا “worship!”.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_command_how
string-array.item: It is made from the present: drop the prefix, and if the word then starts with a sukūn, put ٱ in front: تَقۡرَأُ, قۡرَأۡ, ٱقۡرَأۡ.
It always speaks to “you”: one man, one woman (وَٱرۡكَعِي, 3:43) or a group.
From Allah to people it is a command; from people to Allah, as in ٱهۡدِنَا, it is a prayer.

resources.string: The command not to do something uses لَا and a present verb: لَا تَقۡهَرۡ “do not oppress”.
So as for the orphan, do not oppress him (fa-ammā l-yatīma fa-lā taqhar)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_prohibition_spot
string-array.item: لَا, then a present verb with تَـ, ending in a sukūn: لَا تَقۡهَرۡ.
To a group, ـُونَ becomes ـُوا: وَلَا تَعۡتَدُوٓاْ “and do not transgress” (2:190).

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_prohibition_how
string-array.item: It is the opposite of a command: “do not …”.
This لَا puts the verb in jazm, so its ending is cut short.
From people to Allah it is a prayer: رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذۡنَآ “our Lord, do not take us to task” (2:286).

resources.string: With a verb in its usual ḍamma, لَا only denies: لَآ أَعۡبُدُ “I do not worship” (109:2).
nor was He begotten (wa lam yūlad)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_passive_spot
string-array.item: Past: a ḍamma on the first letter and a kasra before the last: خُلِقَ “was created”.
Present: a ḍamma on the prefix and a fatḥa before the last: يُولَدۡ “is begotten”.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_passive_how
string-array.item: The doer is left out, and what was acted on takes its place, in rafʿ: وَخُلِقَ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنُ “and man was created” (4:28).
The doer may be obvious, unknown, or not the point.
Compare يَلِدۡ “He begets” with يُولَدۡ “He is begotten”: the vowels change who does what.

resources.string: مَغۡضُوب “the one angered at” is a passive noun, not a verb: it takes ال and has no time.
Indeed, mankind is in loss (inna l-insāna la-fī khusr)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_inna_spot
string-array.item: إِنَّ “indeed”, أَنَّ “that”, لَٰكِنَّ “but”, كَأَنَّ “as if”, لَيۡتَ “if only”, لَعَلَّ “perhaps, so that”.
The noun after it is in naṣb: ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_inna_how
string-array.item: It comes before a nominal sentence: a subject and what is said about it.
Its subject goes into naṣb; what is said about it stays in rafʿ.
The لَـ in لَفِي adds more stress: “surely in loss”.

resources.string: Kāna does the mirror image: its subject stays in rafʿ, and what is said about it goes into naṣb.
and there is none equal to Him (wa lam yakun lahū kufuwan aḥad)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_kana_spot
string-array.item: كَانَ “was”, أَصۡبَحَ “became (by morning)”, صَارَ “became”, لَيۡسَ “is not”, مَا زَالَ “still”.
What is said about the subject is in naṣb: كُفُوًا.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_kana_how
string-array.item: It comes before a nominal sentence and places it in time: وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلِيمًا “and Allah is ever Knowing” (4:17).
Its subject stays in rafʿ (أَحَدٌ); what is said about it goes into naṣb (كُفُوًا).
The order can change: here كُفُوًا comes before أَحَدٌ, and the endings still tell you which is which.

resources.string: Inna does the mirror image: its subject goes into naṣb, and what is said about it stays in rafʿ.
no doubt in it (lā rayba fīh)

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_la_generic_spot
string-array.item: لَا, then straight away an indefinite noun,
ending in a fatḥa with no tanwīn: لَا رَيۡبَ.

string-array.name: grammar_lesson_la_generic_how
string-array.item: It denies every one of its kind: not a single doubt.
It works like إِنَّ: its noun is in naṣb, shown by a fatḥa without tanwīn.
The testimony of faith uses it: لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ “there is no god but Allah” (47:19).

resources.string: With tanwīn it is an ordinary “no”: لَّا بَيۡعٞ فِيهِ “no trading in it” (2:254).
